title: A quantum computer can work and still be a dead end
source_used: CTech by Calcalist (article text read from the page's embedded article data)
key_facts: Opinion piece by Dr. Guy Raz, co-founder, CEO and CTO of Q-Factor, published 2 Oct 2026 in Calcalist's CTech.
He argues the next quantum hardware race will be decided by scaling overhead: control, calibration, readout and error correction have to grow along with the number of qubits.
He says a design can fail even if every part works, because running the parts together becomes too complex; even modular designs can be held back by the links between modules.
He says neutral atoms are the most promising platform for the coming scaling phase.

He cites a Caltech array of 6,100 neutral-atom qubits and a Harvard-led team using up to 448 qubits for repeated error correction; the large arrays and the key fault-tolerant operations have been shown only separately.

He says Q-Factor, building on research at the Weizmann Institute and the Technion, is designing a much larger single atomic core aimed at the million-qubit scale, and has developed a method to reverse heating caused by two-qubit gates.
He says Q-Factor researchers and collaborators propose using helper atoms to improve readout, supported by simulations.
quote_evidence: The next quantum hardware race will be decided by scaling overhead.
In the race to one million qubits, the challenge is not only getting there, but making sure the rest of the machine can scale with them.
why_it_matters_hint: A company founder names the control and readout burden as the main obstacle to very large quantum computers, but the piece also promotes his own design.
event_date: Published 2 Oct 2026; opinion piece, no single event.
notes: Opinion by the CEO of a company that sells the approach it favours; not an independent finding and no new test results. The page returned HTTP 200 but the article body sits in embedded JSON, which was used.
